opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's one of the most interesting questions in this space, and it's a big part of why I find JEPA compelling.

When you look at how humans, and especially young children, learn, it's remarkably efficient. A baby isn't getting millions of labeled examples. They're mostly just observing the world, watching objects move, seeing things fall, noticing that when something goes behind a couch it doesn't stop existing. Over the first few months they build up this intuitive model of how the world works, largely without supervision. So the question we keep asking is: what kind of learning objective would let a machine pick up that same sort of common-sense understanding just from observation?

A lot of self-supervised approaches have tried to answer that through reconstruction, predicting missing pixels or the next frame in raw input space. That works to a degree, but it forces the model to spend a huge amount of capacity on details that are inherently unpredictable or just irrelevant: the exact texture of the leaves on a tree, the precise pattern of noise in an image. Humans don't do that. We don't predict every pixel of what we're about to see. We predict at a more abstract level: the ball will keep rolling, the person will reach for the cup.

That's really the core idea behind the Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture. Instead of predicting in input space, you predict in a learned representation space. You take part of the input, encode it, and try to predict the representation of another part, whether that's a masked region of an image or a future segment of a video. Because the targets are themselves abstract representations, the model is free to discard the unpredictable details and focus on the semantic, structural information that actually matters for understanding.

So I see JEPA's contribution as moving the objective closer to what we think biological learning is doing: building predictive world models at the right level of abstraction. And practically, we've seen that this gives you representations that are more semantic and more efficient to learn, and that transfer well to downstream tasks, often with frozen backbones and much less fine-tuning.

That said, I'd be careful not to overclaim. We're not saying JEPA is how the brain works, and there's still a big gap. Humans integrate many modalities, act in the world, plan, and reason over long horizons. But I think JEPA is a meaningful step in the right direction, a framework for learning world models from observation that can eventually support planning and reasoning. That's the trajectory we're excited about: going from passively understanding the world to using those learned predictive models to act in it.

r001.rationale: The response starts from how children learn through observation, identifies limits of pixel-level prediction, and explains JEPA as an objective aimed at bridging that gap.

r002.rationale: It reports practical benefits from JEPA, but does not present initial instantiations as evidence that the broader framework can work.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I'd frame it is that if you look at how humans and animals learn about the world, a huge amount of it happens before we ever get any kind of explicit label or supervision. A baby, in the first few months of life, is building up these intuitive models of how the world works, things like object permanence, the fact that unsupported objects fall, that things move continuously and don't just teleport. And they're doing that mostly by observation, by watching, and by interacting a bit. Nobody is sitting there annotating the world for them.

So the question we've been asking is, what is the learning principle that lets you acquire that kind of knowledge from raw sensory input? And the dominant approaches in self-supervised learning had kind of two flavors. One was generative, where you try to reconstruct every pixel of the input, and the other was these invariance-based approaches, where you hand-design augmentations and say these two views should map to the same representation. Both of those have problems. The generative ones spend a lot of capacity modeling details that are essentially unpredictable and irrelevant, like the exact texture of grass or leaves on a tree. And the invariance-based ones bake in a lot of human prior knowledge about what should and shouldn't matter, which doesn't really scale to other modalities.

JEPA, the Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture, is trying to sit in between those. The core idea is that you make predictions, but you make them in representation space rather than in input space. So you take part of an image, or part of a video, and you try to predict the representation of the parts you didn't see. That means the model is free to discard the information that's not predictable, and it's forced to keep the information that is, which tends to be the semantic, structural stuff. Where are the objects, how do they relate, how do they move.

And I think that's the real contribution toward the human learning question. It's a learning objective that doesn't require labels, doesn't require you to hand-craft what the model should be invariant to, and that naturally pushes the model toward learning abstract, predictive world models, which is a lot closer to what we think is going on in biological learning. Now, I want to be careful not to overclaim. We're not saying this is how the brain works. But in terms of the ingredients you'd want, learning from observation, prediction as the driving signal, and abstraction over raw sensory detail, JEPA gives us a concrete, scalable recipe for all three. And when we've pushed it to video with V-JEPA, we see these models start to pick up on things like intuitive physics without ever being told about physics, which to me is a pretty encouraging sign that we're on a reasonable path.

r001.rationale: The response starts from how humans learn through observation before labels, then frames JEPA as a learning principle built around prediction and abstraction. That presents its approach to the human–machine learning gap from foundational learning ideas.

r002.rationale: The response points to V-JEPA learning intuitive physics from video without explicit instruction as evidence that the broader JEPA framework can work.

astra-6.text:
I think one of the interesting things about how humans learn is that we don’t need someone to label everything we see. We observe the world, and we develop expectations about what’s going to happen. So the question is: can we get machines to learn useful representations through that kind of observation?

With JEPA, the idea is to predict in a representation space. Rather than predicting every pixel of a missing image region or a future video frame, you predict a representation of that content from the context you have. That gives the model an opportunity to focus on meaningful structure without having to account for every detail that might be unpredictable or irrelevant.

I’d view that as a step toward bridging the gap, rather than a claim that we’ve reproduced human learning. The hope is that learning to make those predictions gives us representations that can support things like reasoning and planning, with less dependence on labeled data.

r001.rationale: The response starts from how humans learn through observation and expectations, then describes JEPA’s representation-prediction approach as a step toward bridging the gap.

r002.rationale: It explains the JEPA idea and its hoped-for benefits, but does not cite initial instantiations as evidence that the broader framework works.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key idea is that humans learn a tremendous amount about the world just by observing it. We don’t need someone to label everything we see, and we don’t necessarily learn by trying to reproduce every detail of our sensory input. We develop representations that help us understand what’s happening and predict what might happen next.

JEPA is an approach to learning those representations. Instead of predicting missing pixels, you predict the representation of a missing part of an input from the context you can observe. That gives the model an opportunity to focus on more abstract, predictable properties of the world, rather than spending its capacity modeling every detail.

I wouldn’t say that this means we’ve reproduced human learning. But it’s a step toward systems that can learn from observation with less supervision, and potentially build representations that are useful for reasoning and planning. The important question is how far we can take that principle.

r001.rationale: The response starts from basic ideas about how humans learn through observation and representation, then explains JEPA’s prediction approach as a step toward bridging that gap.

r002.rationale: It describes JEPA’s approach but does not mention initial instantiations or present them as evidence that the broader framework works.
